1.title: Evaluating Foundation Models
1.text: Welcome to Module ten: Evaluating Foundation Models. This module covers task statement three point four, and it closes Domain three. You will learn how to tell whether a model, a R A G system or an agent is good enough, with datasets, approaches and metrics. The exam gives you a situation and asks you to name the right approach or the right metric.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do four things. Choose an evaluation approach: human-in-the-loop, benchmark datasets and Amazon Bedrock Model Evaluation. Pick a metric: Rouge, Bleu, Bert Score and L L M as a judge. Judge whether a model meets business objectives. And evaluate R A G, agents and workflows, using business alignment metrics.

1.title: Case Check-In: Cedar and Salt Tests Before Launch
1.text: At Cedar and Salt Travel, leaders will launch the assistant only if it is good enough. The team has candidate models, a knowledge base and an agent to compare. Reviewers disagree on tone, and thousands of answers are too many to read. Your job is to pick the approach and the metrics that prove it.

1.title: Why Evaluate, and with What Data
1.text: Evaluation is the most critical and challenging part of building generative A I, because outputs are unstructured and subjective. Use a mix: automated metrics, model-based scoring and human review. Start with a golden dataset of question and answer pairs, ideally curated by people. Good sources are real logs, expert-written examples, and synthetic data that you check carefully. Ground truth can be a reference text, or a list of expected facts. And choose metrics that fit the business problem. Exam tip: one metric is never enough, so combine automated, model-based and human evaluation.

1.title: Benchmark Datasets and Built-In Tasks
1.text: Amazon Bedrock offers built-in tasks and benchmark datasets. For text summarization, the dataset is Gigaword, and the accuracy measure is Bert Score. For question and answer, the datasets are Bool Q, Natural Questions and Trivia Q A, with an F one score. For text classification, it uses a clothing reviews dataset, with classification accuracy. And for general text generation, T Rex, with a real world knowledge score. Amazon Bedrock also scores robustness and toxicity. You can use a built-in dataset or your own custom prompt dataset. Exam tip: a benchmark dataset gives a fair, repeatable test, and a custom dataset tests your use case.

1.title: Evaluation Approaches in Amazon Bedrock
1.text: The picture shows four evaluation approaches in Amazon Bedrock. Programmatic evaluation computes scores on a built-in or custom dataset. Human evaluation uses a work team of your employees or subject-matter experts to rate the answers. A judge model evaluation uses a second L L M to score each answer and explain why. And R A G evaluation checks a knowledge base for retrieval and for answers. Exam tip: Amazon Bedrock Model Evaluation covers automatic, human, judge-model and R A G evaluations.

1.title: ROUGE and BLEU
1.text: Two classic metrics compare generated text with a reference. Rouge stands for Recall-Oriented Understudy for Gisting Evaluation. It measures n-gram overlap with the reference, focusing on recall, and it is typical for summarization and question answering. Bleu stands for Bilingual Evaluation Understudy. It also measures n-gram overlap, but focuses on precision, and penalizes outputs that are too short; it is typical for machine translation. Both are fast, cheap and objective, and both need a reference text. Both miss meaning, and penalize valid rephrasing. Exam tip: recall and summaries mean Rouge; precision and translation mean Bleu.

1.title: BERTScore
1.text: Bert Score compares the embeddings of the generated text and the reference text. So it measures semantic similarity, and a paraphrase can still score well. It captures meaning better than word overlap, but it costs more compute. It also needs a reference text. Amazon Bedrock uses Bert Score as the accuracy measure for summarization. Meteor is another overlap metric, and it also credits synonyms and stems. Exam tip: same meaning in different words means Bert Score.

1.title: LLM-as-a-Judge
1.text: With L L M as a judge, a second L L M, the judge, scores another model's answers and explains each score. The job needs a generator model and an evaluator model. The built-in metrics are correctness, completeness, faithfulness, helpfulness, coherence, relevance, following instructions, tone, harmfulness, stereotyping and refusal. You can also add custom metrics. It is faster and cheaper than people, but a judge can be biased. So use a judge from a different model family, validate it against people, and keep humans for critical decisions. Exam tip: scoring thousands of answers with explanations means L L M as a judge.

1.title: Human-in-the-Loop Evaluation
1.text: People are the ultimate source of truth for quality. In Amazon Bedrock, the work team can be your employees or subject-matter experts. They rate answers on a scale, or compare two outputs. This is best for subjective qualities, such as tone, style and brand voice. The downsides are that it is slow, expensive and sometimes inconsistent. Use people to build the golden dataset, to audit the judge, and to act as the final quality gate. Exam tip: for subjective quality, such as tone, add human evaluation.

1.title: Evaluating RAG, Agents and Workflows
1.text: R A G has two kinds of evaluation. Retrieve only asks: does the knowledge base fetch relevant passages? Retrieve and generate asks: is the final answer correct, complete and faithful to the sources? Both need a dataset with ground truth, the expected texts and responses. For agents, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations scores an agent's traces with built-in or custom evaluators, using L L M as a judge. For workflows, evaluate each step, not only the final result. As of five November twenty twenty-six, AgentCore Evaluations works with frameworks such as Strands and LangGraph. Exam tip: judge the retrieval step and the answer step separately.

1.title: Do the Results Meet Business Objectives?
1.text: Does the system meet business objectives? Five business alignment metrics matter. Productivity: the time or effort saved per task. User engagement: how often and how long people use it. Task completion rate: the share of tasks the assistant finishes successfully. User satisfaction: how users rate their experience. And cost per interaction: the A I cost per conversation or request. Pair model metrics, such as Rouge and Bert Score, with business metrics. Exam tip: a good Rouge score does not prove business value. Task completion and satisfaction do.

1.title: What the Exam Asks: Evaluation
1.text: Here is how the exam frames this module. Which approach: human-in-the-loop, a benchmark dataset, Amazon Bedrock Model Evaluation, or a judge model. Which metric: Rouge for summaries, Bleu for translation, Bert Score for meaning, and L L M as a judge for scale. Which target: a model, a R A G system, an agent or a workflow. And which business measure: productivity, engagement, task completion, satisfaction or cost per interaction. Exam tip: name what you are judging first, then the approach and the metric.

1.title: Design Check: Cedar and Salt's Launch Review
1.text: Now a design check. Cover the right column and name the answer. Compare summaries with reference summaries by word overlap: Rouge. Check a translated policy against a human translation: Bleu. Summaries paraphrase the reference but mean the same: Bert Score. Score thousands of answers quickly, with reasons: L L M as a judge. Judge the warmth of the tone: human evaluation. Check that the knowledge base fetches the right passages: R A G evaluation, retrieve only. And show the assistant helps guests book: task completion rate and satisfaction. Pause the video if you want more time.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. The approaches are benchmark datasets, human-in-the-loop, a judge model, and Amazon Bedrock Model Evaluation. The metrics are Rouge for recall, Bleu for precision and translation, Bert Score for meaning, and L L M as a judge. The targets are models, R A G systems, agents and workflows, judged step by step. And business alignment uses productivity, engagement, task completion, satisfaction and cost per interaction.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. Which metric measures n-gram overlap with a reference text, focuses on recall, and is commonly used for summarization? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: Rouge. It measures n-gram overlap and focuses on recall, so it suits summarization. Bleu focuses on precision and suits translation, and Bert Score compares embeddings.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. Cedar and Salt's tool writes summaries that paraphrase the reference summaries. Which metric captures the shared meaning better than exact word overlap? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: Bert Score. It compares the embeddings of the generated and reference text, so it measures semantic similarity and gives credit to paraphrases. Rouge and Bleu depend on matching words.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. Select two. Which two statements about Rouge and Bleu are correct? The five options are on the screen. The answers are A and C. Rouge is recall-oriented and used for summaries. Bleu is precision-oriented and used for machine translation. Both compare generated text with a reference text, and neither measures toxicity.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. Cedar and Salt must score thousands of assistant answers quickly, with an explanation for each score. Which approach fits best? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: run a job that uses a judge model to score the answers. A judge model scores each response and explains the score, and it scales far better than human review. Keep people for subjective or critical decisions.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. Which statement describes a benefit of human-in-the-loop evaluation of a foundation model? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: it judges subjective qualities, such as tone, better than fixed metrics. People are best at tone, style and brand voice, and they calibrate automatic and judge scores. Human review is slower, costlier and can vary between reviewers.

1.title: Practice Question 6
1.text: Question six. Leaders ask whether the booking assistant meets the company's business objectives. Which measures fit best? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: task completion rate and user satisfaction. Business alignment metrics include productivity, engagement, task completion, satisfaction and cost per interaction. Rouge and Bleu score text quality, and model size does not measure business results.

1.title: Answers at a Glance
1.text: Here are all six answers. Question one: B. Question two: C. Question three: A and C. Question four: D. Question five: A. Question six: C. That completes Module ten, and Domain three. Next, Module eleven opens Domain four, with guidelines for responsible A I.
